*Big Tech & Startups*
*Apple Announces Oct. 28 Event for Touch-Screen MacBook Pro (2 minute read)*


Apple will be holding a product launch event on October 28 to debut its
first touch-screen MacBook. The company will also introduce a new low-end
MacBook Pro with an M6 chip, a refreshed iMac, and a revamped iPad mini
with a sharper screen. Apple retail stores are preparing to begin selling
new products on November 6. The new touch MacBooks, which will run on M5
Pro and M5 Max chips, will have a Dynamic Island interface, as well as a
sharper OLED display.
*Waymo plans to quintuple its fleet (1 minute read)*


Waymo plans to grow its fleet to 20,000 by the end of next year. It
recently raised $5 billion from private credit lenders to achieve this
goal. The company has already ordered thousands of cars from China to help
expand its fleet. Waymo currently operates 4,000 vehicles in 15 cities in
the US.
🚀
*Science & Futuristic Technology*
*AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now? (6 minute read)*


The quasi-Riemann hypothesis is a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis,
arguably the biggest open question in math. Resolving the Riemann
hypothesis would enable mathematicians to better understand the nature of
prime numbers. OpenAI's recently released proof for the quasi-Riemann
hypothesis is the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite
a margin. The vast majority of the consequences of resolving it already
follow from solving the quasi-Riemann hypothesis.
*Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in “proof point” test (11
minute read)*


Endurance Energy, a Seattle-based startup, recently demonstrated the
technical feasibility of using an active underwater volcano to generate
electricity. The startup deployed a 3-ton prototype power plant at the
Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September and generated
less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity. The company's next trial
run, planned for the winter of 2026 to 2027, will aim to sustain higher
power generation. It is currently developing a 2-megawatt commercial
generator for its first planned commercial deployment with the Kingdom of
Tonga in 2027.

Get the whitepaper

*Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models (16
minute read)*


Clairic is an extraction model. Extraction models are a new class of System
One-style models that can extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values
from unstructured inputs, all at significantly higher accuracy, faster
latency, and lower cost than traditional LLMs. It answers with values
directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond
it. The model can't produce a mistyped answer or hallucinate in the same
way an LLM can, but it can still make mistakes.
*Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
(15 minute read)*


Cloudflare lowered its average review cost from $2.43 to $0.77. The biggest
single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each
session's first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way
that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests, and
repositories. Check whether each session's first request actually reads
from the cache and whether reviewers still find real problems at the effort
level being paid for.
🎁
*Miscellaneous*
*AI will not automate radiologists like you think (6 minute read)*


Some worry about radiology being totally automated, but the more likely
outcome is a future where there is more demand for services as predictive
power increases. This is similar to how programming is thriving despite
drastic change in the field. It may be possible one day to use radiology
images to predict disease probabilities far into the future. Any domain
where demand can be elastic and quality can scale with increased
intelligence will similarly flourish with the development of AI.
*Saudis Aided Family of Engineer Accused of Bugging OpenAI, Prosecutors Say
(6 minute read)*


Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan was recently arrested and
charged after a hidden recording device in one of OpenAI's offices was
traced back to him. The engineer was in frequent contact with a member of
the Saudi royal family, who was trying to recruit him to work in Saudi
Arabia, but Alfozan had refused, saying he wanted to collect the company
stock he had been promised. The Saudi government has offered to pay his
bail, and a member of the Saudi military paid for his wife and infant son
to fly out of the US the day after his arrest.
